Reel
reel
v.i. (to stagger; to incline in walking, first to one side then the other, as a drunken man)
Saxon hreol, a reel or winding frame; hence the verb, to whirl or stagger. Both Scripture uses pair it with the figure of a drunkard.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences pair the word with drunkenness, and both describe a loss of footing that is not the walker's fault alone. The first is the great storm passage of Psalm 107: mariners caught in a tempest “reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end” (Psa 107:27). The Hebrew behind wits' end says literally that all their wisdom was swallowed up — competent seamen with nothing left to try. The next verse is the turn: “Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses” (Psa 107:28). The crying comes at the end of the resources, and the psalm treats that as the normal order rather than a failure. The second occurrence is cosmic: “The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again” (Isa 24:20). The planet itself staggers under the weight of its own transgression. Paul uses the same instability of Christians who have no doctrinal footing: “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reel as to stagger; to incline or move in walking, first to one side and then to the other; to vacillate; and notes it of a drunken man or of one who is dizzy.

REEL, v.i.

To stagger; to incline or move in walking, first to one side and then to the other; to vacillate.

He reels with weariness or drunkenness.

They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man. Ps. 107.

REEL, n. [Sax. hreol.] A frame or machine turning on an axis, on which yarn is extended for winding.

Key Scripture

Psalm 107:27 — "They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end."

Isaiah 24:20 — "The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again."

Psalm 107:28 — "Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses."

Ephesians 4:14 — "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;"

Modern Corruption

Doctrinal instability is now described as openness, and a church with no footing is praised for being teachable.

expand to see more

Ephesians 4:14 describes a congregation reeling — tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine — and Paul treats it as childishness to be outgrown, not humility to be admired. The contemporary translation of the condition is generous: such a church is exploratory, non-dogmatic, willing to hold things loosely. Paul names the mechanism instead: the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive. Somebody is steering. A body that will move with any wind is not free; it is available, and the apostle assumes someone is waiting to take it. The remedy he gives in the same passage is not less teaching but more — pastors and teachers, until the whole body comes to the unity of the faith.

Psalm 107:27 puts the other kind of reeling in a far kinder light. These are sailors in a real storm, and they reel because the sea is doing it to them; the psalm does not scold them for having exhausted their seamanship. It simply notes that at their wits' end they cried, and He brought them out. That is the pattern for every believer whose footing is gone through affliction rather than through drift. Isaiah 24:20 then sets the whole creation staggering under the weight of transgression, and even there the chapter ends with the LORD of hosts reigning in Zion. The earth reels; the throne does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chagag (H2287), to reel, to move in a circle; nua (H5128), to totter, wander; chokmatham tithballa, their wisdom is swallowed up.

expand to see more

Hebrew yachoggu (H2287) — they reel, go round; Psalm 107:27, from a root also meaning to keep a festival by circling.

Hebrew nua tanua (H5128) — reeling it shall reel; Isaiah 24:20, the doubled verb of the staggering earth.

Hebrew kol chokmatham tithballa (H2451, H1104) — all their wisdom is swallowed up; the literal of at their wits' end.

Greek kludonizomenoi (G2831) — tossed by waves; Ephesians 4:14, the same instability applied to doctrine.

Saxon hreol — a winding frame; Webster's root, whence the whirling sense of the verb.

Usage

"“Reel to and fro… and are at their wits' end” — all their wisdom swallowed up."

"“Then they cry unto the LORD” — at the end of the resources, and the psalm expects it."

"“Carried about with every wind of doctrine” — and somebody is working the wind."
